articles.title_orig: Track where a potent nor’easter will bring heavy rain, winds and waves
articles.title_zh: Track where a potent nor’easter will bring heavy rain, winds and waves
articles.content_orig:
Millions across the Northeast are bracing for an intense, multi-day Nor’easter this weekend that is forecast to bring heavy rain and strong wind gusts to the East Coast.
Forecast models still disagree on the storm’s exact track, but one thing is clear: wherever it goes, it will hit the region hard. Forecasters have high confidence in a long-duration onshore wind event that could bring significant coastal flooding.
Coastal flood warnings and high wind watches are already in place along much of the East Coast, with more alerts likely to be issued throughout the day Thursday.
The highest rainfall totals — 2 to 3 inches or more — are most likely from Rhode Island to eastern Massachusetts.
Powerful winds, including gusts up to 50-60 mph, risk toppling power lines and trees. Small shifts in the storm’s track will determine where outages and downed trees are most likely to occur.
Coastal flooding is expected to run 1 to 3 feet above high tide, and a full moon Saturday night could intensify the tides and worsen the flooding. Waves along the coast are expected to reach 12 feet in Ocean City, New Jersey, and up to 22 feet in New England.
Moderate to major flooding is likely from North Carolina to Nantucket, Massachusetts, with southeastern Virginia — particularly the Virginia Beach-to-Norfolk area — at highest risk for major coastal inundation of 1 to 3 feet.
Meanwhile, a separate storm is already pummeling the Eastern Seaboard, generating high winds and rough surf.
In Massachusetts, residents were seen this week hauling their boats out of the bay, worried about high tides and flooding from the Nor’easter. One person told NBC News he’d been “prepping all week for both wind and water.”
One couple even changed their wedding plans because of the storm — they had been set to marry this weekend on a Massachusetts beach.
And the Boston Red Sox moved Sunday’s game — the season finale — up to Friday to avoid any weather-related delays or cancellations.
In New Jersey, crews cleared debris from storm drains and flood-prone areas as emergency management officials urged residents to prepare for the incoming storm. Monmouth County Sheriff Shaun Golden recommended charging devices and stocking up on batteries ahead of possible power outages.
Elsewhere in the country, days of heavy rain in the Southwest have triggered major flooding, sending muddy waters sweeping through the streets of New Mexico. The El Paso, Texas, fire department said it has responded to more than 50 storm-related calls.
Off the coast of Hawaii’s Big Island, Tropical Storm Nolo threatens heavy rain and flash flooding, with more than 30 inches of rain  possible in some areas. Extreme rainfall remains the storm’s biggest risk.
Nolo currently has sustained winds of 50 mph and is expected to strengthen into a hurricane by Thursday night — potentially reaching Category 3 strength. As of the latest update, the storm was about 285 miles south of South Point, Hawaii, moving north at 2 mph.
Nolo is not expected to make direct landfall in Hawaii, but it could come close enough to bring tropical-storm-force winds to the Big Island and Maui as early as Thursday night, with hurricane-force winds possible by Friday night.
Rebecca Cohen is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Sam Brock is an NBC News correspondent.

articles.title_zh: Stock futures slide again as Treasury yields push higher, Oracle leads Nasdaq names lower: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Oracle shares fell 4% on Thursday following news that the company sent a "force majeure" notice tied to its New Mexico data center project to protect itself from higher expenses.
"Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule," an Oracle said in a statement to CNBC. "We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward."
Bloomberg was first to report the news, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The company is looking to delay payment on the campus, dubbed Project Jupiter, if it doesn't come online as expected in 2028, according to the report.
Oracle sent the notice to the developer, which is a unit of Blue Owl Capital . The company also saw its shares fall on Thursday.
"This notice does not change the financial commitments to this multi-year project," Blue Owl Capital said in a statement to CNBC.
The New Mexico data center project, which is part of the broader Stargate artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout with President Donald Trump , has been riddled with setbacks and regulatory hurdles.
That includes local opposition to data centers ahead of the upcoming midterm elections and concerns from environmental groups.
Concerns have also mounted over Oracle's $18 billion in debt tied to the datacenter, which is already trading at stressed levels, according to the Financial Times.
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Leslie Picker contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Starbucks to close 250 stores: 'Difficult decision'
articles.title_zh: Starbucks to close 250 stores: 'Difficult decision'
articles.content_orig:
Starbucks on Thursday announced it will close about 1% of its North American cafes as part of its turnaround.
Under CEO Brian Niccol, Starbucks has staged a revamp of its U.S. business that has focused on improving the customer experience, including in-person interactions at its cafes. The announcement marks the second round of closures in North America during Niccol's two-year tenure.
Starbucks expects to shutter about 250 underperforming cafes out of its more than 18,000 locations in North America. It was not immediately clear where the closing locations are.
"We have carefully reviewed our North America coffeehouse portfolio and identified locations where we do not believe we can consistently deliver the experience we want for customers and partners or where we don't see a path to acceptable financial performance," Mike Grams, Starbucks chief operating officer, wrote in a letter addressed to employees.
For fiscal 2026, Starbucks is now projecting net new openings of 440 cafes, down from its prior outlook of 600 to 650 locations. Those new cafes will come from its international markets.
"The Company continues to see significant longer-term growth opportunity ahead in North America and is actively developing a strong pipeline of new coffeehouses," Starbucks said in a regulatory filing .
Most of the closures will occur before the end of fiscal 2026, according to the filing. Starbucks' fiscal year ends later this month.
The company expects to incur about $300 million in restructuring charges related to the closures. About $200 million of that charge will be related to the costs of exiting leases early and paying employees separation benefits. The remaining $100 million will be noncash charges from the disposal and impairment of its company-owned restaurant assets.

articles.title_zh: Fury vs Joshua: Cardiff to host heavyweight fight on 11 December
articles.content_orig:
Tyson Fury will face Anthony Joshua in an all-British heavyweight showdown in Cardiff on December 11.
The long-awaited clash had initially been linked with venues in New York and London before promoters settled on the Principality Stadium in the Welsh capital.
After months of negotiations that threatened to scupper the fight, as Fury called for a rematch with Oleksandr Usyk , Saudi Arabian boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh announced the venue and date for the bout on Thursday.
“For 15 years no one has been able to make this fight,” he wrote on social media.
“Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. The time for talking is over…”
Choosing the 80,000-capacity stadium in Cardiff, which has hosted the Champions League and FA Cup finals, as well as Wales national team matches in football and rugby, allows both fighters to finally start their preparations for the eagerly anticipated clash.
The fight, one of the biggest in British boxing history, will be broadcast on streaming service Netflix.
Fury, 37, defeated 46-year-old Mariusz Wach in Thailand in his most recent bout in July.
Joshua, 36, survived a pair of first-round knockdowns to beat the unheralded Kristian Prenga in his last fight two months ago.

articles.content_orig:
Taylor Swift will debut her music video for "Patient Zero" at the MTV Video Music Awards this Sunday.
A 13-second preview clip of the music video aired exclusively on "CBS Mornings" Thursday. Swift considers 13 her lucky number.
Swift announced "Patient Zero" earlier this week, saying on social media she has been "impatiently waiting" to announce the new single will be out on Friday. A new deluxe version of her latest album, with four new songs, "The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore," is also out on Friday.
The "Patient Zero" music video features actors Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson and the cinematography was done by Academy Award winner Emmanuel Lubezski.
The VMAs will mark a milestone for Swift, who will be given the VMAs' first-ever Artist Director Honors, which organizers said recognizes artists "whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling."
The new accolade guarantees Swift, who is also nominated in 11 categories, will become the show's most-awarded artist, breaking the tie between her and Beyoncé.
The VMAs air on CBS television stations and MTV beginning at 7:30 p.m. ET, 4:30 p.m. PT., on Sunday, Sept. 27. The show will also be streaming on Paramount+ .

articles.title_orig: Navy says 8 sailors attempted suicide aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln
articles.title_zh: Navy says 8 sailors attempted suicide aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln
articles.content_orig:
There have been eight suicide attempts across the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group since the beginning of its grueling monthslong deployment last year, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said in a letter obtained by CBS News.
That number includes sailors assigned to the Lincoln aircraft carrier, its air wing and the destroyers that are escorting the ship, Cao wrote in response to questions from Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York. No suicides have taken place onboard.
A defense official told CBS News two of the suicide attempts occurred during active fighting with Iran. The letter covers the entire length of the Lincoln strike group's deployment, which began in November of last year.
CNN was first to report the figures. A Navy official confirmed the letter was sent Tuesday.
The Lincoln and its thousands of crew members have been deployed for more than nine months, including more than 250 uninterrupted days at sea this year. Much of that time was spent in the Middle East, where the carrier strike group supported the U.S. war against Iran.
During its record-long time at sea, the aircraft carrier faced reports of food shortages , supply issues and faulty plumbing. The families of crew members also raised concerns about deteriorating mental health among the sailors and Marines assigned to the Lincoln, drawing alarm from congressional Democrats.
"What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," Gillibrand said in a statement Wednesday.
The Pentagon has defended conditions on the ship, saying there has not been an increase in suicide attempts and personnel have access to counselors, chaplains and other support.
Asked for comment, the Navy referred CBS News to a video that Cao posted to X over the weekend. The Navy's top civilian official addressed mental health, saying: "We must confront the rising tide of suicide head-on."
His wife, April, also appeared in the video and encouraged people to speak up about any challenges.
The Lincoln left the Middle East late last month after it was relieved by the USS George Washington , and it docked in Thailand in early September. The carrier arrived in Guam earlier this week, as it sails in the direction of its home port of San Diego.
Cao told Gillibrand the Lincoln's exact schedule and plans to return to its home port are classified, but he confirmed reports that it was relieved of its duties in the Middle East.
If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here . For more information about mental health care resources and support , The National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m.–10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org .

articles.title_orig: Block the Merger Coalition Files Legal Request to Oppose Paramount-Warner Bros. Deal
articles.title_zh: Block the Merger Coalition Files Legal Request to Oppose Paramount-Warner Bros. Deal
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Tensions flared on the eve of a critical week ahead for Paramount Skydance’s proposed $111-billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, amid new urgency for talks aimed at settling antitrust litigation brought by California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta and 11 other states.
Over the weekend, opposition intensified to a proposed settlement as details trickled out, including a proposal to establish a bipartisan editorial board to monitor cable news channel CNN, one of Warner’s premier properties that Paramount Chief Executive David Ellison would control along with   CBS News.
It was unclear Sunday whether a proposed settlement would require Paramount to sell off assets — something Bonta repeatedly has insisted upon. Critics of the deal urged Bonta and other state attorneys general to resist pressure to reach a settlement that would allow Ellison’s deal to move forward.
“State Attorneys General, please hang tough against the giant proposed Paramount-Warner Brothers merger,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) wrote on social media late Saturday.
“Paramount, run by the Ellisons, should not own both CBS and CNN. California must not cave and take a deal that leaves both under the same owner,” Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont) wrote .
A resolution would allow David Ellison’s $111-billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery to finalize
Bonta and Ellison have made progress in the talks in recent days , according to four people familiar with the matter  not authorized to speak publicly.
However, New York’s Letitia James and at least two other  attorneys general who joined Bonta’s lawsuit in July privately have expressed reservations about the proposed compromises, believing they don’t go far enough to mitigate concerns about the power Paramount-Warner Bros. would wield over the film and TV industries should the merger go through, according to the people familiar with the matter.
Neither James nor Connecticut’s William Tong is on board with Bonta’s proposed settlement, three knowledgeable people said. A potential split within Bonta’s coalition could be a setback because Bonta needs the other state attorneys general who joined his legal effort to sign off on any deal.
California’s top prosecutor blasts Paramount-Warner Bros. conduct as ‘amateur hour.’
Reached for comment Sunday, a spokesperson for Bonta reiterated a statement from last week.
“Potential settlement talks are confidential,” the statement said. “We cannot confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.”
Paramount maintains its deal to bring HBO, CNN, CBS, TBS, Comedy Central and two legendary film and television studios together would create a stronger company that could withstand the fierce competition from tech giants such as Apple, Netflix, Google (which owns YouTube) and Amazon. The two studios, on their own, would not be strong enough  to remain viable in the streaming age, the company has said.
On Thursday, Paramount lawyers plan to demand that U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Oakland require the states and the Writers Guild of America to post a $1.88-billion bond that would cover some of Paramount’s delay-related deal costs should the company eventually prevail.
The states and the WGA, which also sued to block the merger, have balked at the request, which was designed by Paramount to create fissures within the coalition of states, which also include Minnesota, Oregon, Colorado, Connecticut, New Jersey and Massachusetts.
Los Angeles’ identity and workers’ livelihoods are at stake, say worried residents who fear that Paramount will leave the state.
Ellison wants the merger finalized by Oct. 1, when his company will be obligated to make a higher payout to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders. The company has threatened to move its Hollywood base from its historic Melrose Avenue lot to Tennessee or Texas should the antitrust battle stretch into October.
The prospective loss of an iconic California business — a century-old film studio that helped establish Hollywood — has rattled state and local politicians, who are fearful of losing more jobs at a time when Los Angeles film production levels already are at alarming lows.
Gov. Gavin Newsom, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for California governor, have  publicly called on Bonta to settle the suit rather than prepare for a trial next spring. City Councilmember Nithya Raman, Bass’ opponent in the L.A. mayor race, has been one of few California politicians in support of Bonta’s fight.
Paramount’s board has approved David Ellison’s contingency plan to move headquarters from Hollywood as early as this fall, according to people familiar with the situation.
In an opinion essay Sunday, a trio of 1st Amendment and antitrust experts dismissed Paramount’s threat to leave Los Angeles as a ploy that doesn’t make business sense.
“Ellison’s threat is empty, and the AG should call that out — not give into it,” the experts — Fiona Scott Morton, Gene Kimmelman and Norm Eisen — wrote in the Contrarian .
Both Morton, an economics professor at the Yale School of Management, and Kimmelman formerly served in the U.S. Justice Department during Democratic administrations. Eisen, founder of the group Democracy Defenders Action, is helping lead the Block the Merger campaign.
“Paramount [would be] sinking the cost of moving before it knows what businesses it owns and how best to combine and organize them — which makes expensive strategic mistakes inevitable,” the trio wrote. “A company that raises its own costs while leaving behind the most valuable labor in the industry does not threaten California; it threatens itself.”
The group noted Paramount, in its regulatory filings, still lists its Times Square offices in New York as its corporate headquarters — not its Melrose Avenue campus in Hollywood.
“There is also the possibility that Ellison is planning to move Paramount to Tennessee regardless of how the lawsuit resolves,” the group wrote.
Bonta and Paramount have discussed including in any settlement a condition that Paramount would keep its operations in California for a set period, according to people familiar with the proposal but not authorized to comment.
Merger opponents planned a Sunday evening rally outside Bonta’s offices in Oakland to encourage him to stand tough. The group plans subsequent demonstrations this week outside James’ office in New York City and the Paramount lot in Hollywood.
The jockeying comes as President Trump, who favors the Ellison takeover of CNN and Warner Bros.,  has barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds because of reporting he dislikes.
“Trump just locked CNN out of the White House. Now his billionaire allies want to own it,” Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) added in a Sunday post . “State attorneys general: Don’t settle. Hold the line. Block this merger.”

articles.title_orig: Trump Aides Seek to Jump-Start Diplomacy With Iran as Crisis Widens
articles.title_zh: Trump Aides Seek to Jump-Start Diplomacy With Iran as Crisis Widens
articles.content_orig:
FDD’s Behnam Ben Taleblu says Iran’s deeply buried nuclear-linked site poses a growing military challenge as Tehran hardens entrances and rebuilds sensitive facilities.
New satellite imagery shows Iran has added new defenses around tunnel entrances at Pickaxe Mountain, the deeply buried nuclear-linked site President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike, as Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a U.S.-drafted Security Council resolution aimed at preserving international monitoring of sanctions on Tehran.
The Institute for Science and International Security said in a report released Thursday that satellite imagery from Sept. 11 shows earthen roadblocks remain in place on roads leading to Pickaxe Mountain’s western tunnel portals near the Natanz nuclear complex. The institute said the continued restricted access reinforces its assessment that the facility is not currently being used for normal operations, while assessing that valuable equipment or materials remain inside.
The report also identified additional soil placed over one western tunnel portal and over a nearby cluster of entrances first built in 2007. The institute said the added soil increases the amount of earth protecting the entrances and helps harden them against aerial bombardment.
EXPERTS ‘DEEPLY’ CONCERNED OVER IRAN’S WORK AT UNDERGROUND NUCLEAR SITE
An overview of Iran’s Natanz nuclear complex and nearby Pickaxe Mountain, seen in satellite imagery from Aug. 21, 2026. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Technologies.)
The findings come one week after Trump issued his latest warning over Pickaxe Mountain .
"We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe," Trump told reporters last week. "I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard."
Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of attacking the site. In a July 28 "Fox & Friends" interview highlighted by the White House , Trump said the U.S. was watching Pickaxe closely and knew "exactly what’s going on," adding that Washington could "take out Pickaxe" if diplomacy failed.
Pickaxe Mountain lies roughly two kilometers from Natanz and features multiple tunnel entrances leading into a deeply buried underground complex. Construction began in 2020 following sabotage that damaged an advanced centrifuge assembly facility at Natanz, and Iranian officials subsequently said a replacement underground facility was being built for advanced centrifuge production. Analysts estimate portions of the facility may be buried at least 100 meters beneath the mountain. Iran has said there is no nuclear activity at the site.
TRUMP SAYS US HAS 'MASSIVE' MUNITIONS STOCKPILE, VOWS 'TREASONOUS' LEAKERS BEING HUNTED DOWN
A closer view of tunnel entrances at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear complex, seen in satellite imagery from Aug. 21, 2026. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Technologies)
Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that some analysts believe the opportunity for a straightforward strike on Pickaxe Mountain may already have passed.
"The window to strike Pickaxe Mountain, according to some, has already expired because the regime has dug an underground nuclear facility several times deeper than Fordow," Ben Taleblu said. But he argued that Washington retains military options even if destroying the underground complex itself proves difficult.
"Washington can do what it’s traditionally been able to do with sites that are underground, hardened and fortified, and that’s to bury their entrances and raise the political cost to the Islamic Republic of being able to dig out," he said.
"While there may not be the perfect munition just yet, Uncle Sam always has a bigger bomb," Ben Taleblu added. "And in the meantime, what they can do is show that they mean business by burying the entrances."
NUCLEAR EXPERTS URGE TRUMP NOT TO LET IRAN STEER TALKS AWAY FROM REGIME'S ATOMIC THREAT
A satellite view shows an overview of the Natanz nuclear facility and Pickaxe Mountain, near Natanz, Iran, June 30, 2026 (Vantor/Handout via Reuters)
The Pickaxe findings came alongside signs of reconstruction at another sensitive Iranian facility .
In a separate report Thursday, the institute said Iran was "rapidly moving forward" with reconstruction of Taleghan 2 at the Parchin military complex southeast of Tehran. Vantor Technologies satellite imagery from Sept. 13 shows Iran erected a tarp over the destroyed hardened facility, obscuring work underneath from satellite or aerial observation, while dump trucks, bulldozers, concrete equipment and cranes were active around the site.
The institute said Iran also built new concrete reinforcement that could provide additional protection against aerial attack. Taleghan 2 was struck by Israel in October 2024 and again in March 2026 after Iran had rebuilt and hardened the facility. The institute said significant questions remain about Tehran’s plans for the site.
The military developments unfolded alongside a separate confrontation over Iran at the United Nations .

The panel investigates alleged sanctions violations and reports on implementation. The dispute reflects a deeper split over whether UN sanctions suspended under the 2015 nuclear agreement were legally restored through the "snapback" mechanism. Most Council members maintain that the sanctions and related monitoring structures were revived, while Russia and China reject the legal and procedural validity of that position.
A day before the vote, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told reporters in New York that Washington considers the sanctions legally restored .
"The snapback sanctions… occurred, the United States and this U.N. Security Council followed appropriate procedures for that to occur," Waltz said Wednesday at a news conference attended by Fox News Digital. "Those sanctions are in place and we expect those who are a party to fully enforce those sanctions."
Waltz said the expert panel is important because sanctioned companies and individuals can attempt to evade restrictions by changing names and corporate structures.
"The president has been clear, and the world community has been clear with resolution after resolution, that the Iranian regime cannot have a nuclear weapon," Waltz said.

articles.title_orig: Accused 105-year-old Nazi POW camp guard under investigation in Germany
articles.title_zh: Accused 105-year-old Nazi POW camp guard under investigation in Germany
articles.content_orig:
A 105-year-old man is being investigated for possible crimes committed at a Nazi prisoner-of-war camp during World War II, German prosecutors said on Thursday.
"The 105-year-old suspect is thought to have been a guard at the prisoner-of-war camp Stalag 326 VI K" in the Senne region of western Germany, prosecutors told AFP in a statement.
The man is "accused of being an accessory to multiple murders through his activities there."
The case was first reported by the Bild newspaper, which said that another former guard at the same camp had recently been investigated but had died in the interim.
The Senne camp housed between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by American troops, according to the memorial which now stands there.
"Of the approximately 5.3 to 5.7 million Soviet prisoners of war who were taken into German captivity overall, between 2.3 and three million did not survive," the memorial says.
Soviet prisoners of war suffered from "malnutrition, inadequate medical care, appalling sanitary conditions, and... forced labor."
Last year prosecutors in Dortmund also opened an investigation into a 100-year-old former guard at another WWII prisoner of war camp in Hemer, which also held mostly Soviet inmates. That man was suspected of taking part in executions between December 1943 and September 1944. Another alleged guard at the camp was charged in 2023 .
Several trials of Nazi camp staff have been held in recent years, spurred by the 2011 conviction of former Sobibor death camp guard John Demjanjuk, despite no proof he had directly killed anyone. Demjanjuk, a former auto worker in the U.S., died in 2012 at the age of 91.
However, time is running out 80 years after the end of the war.
Josef Schuetz, a former guard sentenced in June 2022 to five years in prison, died less than a year later at the age of 102. At the time, he was the oldest person ever to stand trial for crimes committed by the Nazi regime.
In April 2025, an alleged former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp near Berlin died before he could face trial over charges of being complicit in the murder of more than 3,300 people.
In 2021, a 96-year-old woman accused of 11,000 counts of accessory to murder at a Nazi concentration camp went on trial in Germany.
In 2018, former Auschwitz guard Oskar Groening died before he could begin serving his 4-year sentence. Oskar Groening, who was dubbed the " Accountant of Auschwitz ," was convicted in Lueneburg in 2015 as an accessory to the murder of 300,000 Jews. The court concluded that although there was no evidence of involvement in a specific killing, Groening knew that Jews were being slaughtered at the German death camp and supported the killings through his actions.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu expected to attack Mamdani in UN general assembly speech – latest updates
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu expected to attack Mamdani in UN general assembly speech – latest updates
articles.content_orig:
US president may have upstaged the ghost of Soviet leader Khrushchev by musing destruction of fellow member state
Donald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to the United Nations general assembly. But this year, he may have upstaged the ghost of Nikita Khrushchev by openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow UN member state.
Eleven minutes into a 40-minute address, the US president announced he had “a big decision to make” over Iran , which has staged a much more determined resistance than Trump anticipated when he decided to go to war against the country in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild, and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
Possibly not since Khrushchev, the late Soviet leader, brandished his shoe and allegedly banged it on a desk in 1960 in protest at a fellow delegate’s speech has the annual gathering witnessed such a display of bellicosity from a superpower leader.
But this seemed more shocking.
The world may have become inured to Trump’s dire threats to send Iran “to the stone age” or end its civilization – so often have they been issued, only to sometimes be followed by a ceasefire or negotiations. But hearing them voiced in a forum created in the aftermath of the second world war, with the explicit aim of preventing future conflicts, was disconcerting.
Iran was the focal point of much of Trump’s speech, which began with a catalogue of familiar boasts of his supposed achievements that seemed better fitted to a domestic audience.
Whether or not the latest threat should be taken literally, little of what he said about Iran seemed reassuring. He appeared to play fast and loose with the facts, consciously or otherwise.
The US president twice incorrectly asserted that the theocratic regime had held power for 51 years. In fact, the Islamic revolution that toppled the pro-western former Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and installed the current regime happened 47 years ago, in 1979.
Trump also cited apparently inflated figures for the number of Iranians killed in anti-government protests last January, weeks before the war. “The same regime slaughtered over 72,000 of its citizens this year,” he said, in support of his oft-stated declaration that Iran should never be permitted to acquire nuclear weapons.
No definitive death toll has been established. But previous estimates of people killed in the brutal crushing of January’s demonstrations – even including those previously stated by Trump himself – have been much lower.
The ominous rhetoric was not limited to Iran.
Members of the Cuban delegation were seen leaving the hall as he predicted the imminent collapse of the country’s communist regime, which has been struggling to cope with a food security and humanitarian crisis amid tightening US embargoes.
“It’s an absolutely failed state, it’s failing like never before, and it will fall,” Trump said. “Marco Rubio [the US secretary of state] is handling a negotiation. He’s deep into negotiations with Cuba. Let’s see what happens.”
US actions in Venezuela, where special forces last January seized the strongman president, Nicolás Maduro, and spirited him to New York to face drug-trafficking charges, was also cited as an ominous warning to other adversaries – as well as a vocal statement of how the administration would behave in Latin America, Washington’s supposed “back yard”, if it felt its interests threatened.
“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the western hemisphere, and, if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States,” Trump declared.
He was brazenly unabashed in hailing a recent US oil deal with the interim Venezuelan president, Delcy Rodríguez, that he claimed put the US and Venezuela jointly in control of more than 60% of the world’s oil.
“It was perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils – you’ve all heard that,” Trump said.
There was outright antipathy for the international criminal court, which Trump called an “out-of-control institution” and “an evil group of people”. “We will never allow US service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us,” he said.
Given his pugnacious stance towards US adversaries, it probably came as a relief to Washington’s traditional friends that Trump had relatively kind words for them. It was a far cry from his general assembly speech a year ago, when he warned European allies “your countries are all going to hell” because of immigration.
This time, in a pointed message, Trump praised Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, as a “great leader” – a marked departure from his previous denunciations of the military alliance as “obsolete” and a “paper tiger”.
He lauded Denmark as “an incredible, beautiful country”, just days after announcing an agreement with it over Greenland, following prolonged tensions over the territory, which Trump had previously threatened to annex.
With that issue seemingly settled – at least for now – the president declared his intention to flex his muscles on a new battleground: artificial intelligence, or AI.
Echoing recent social media posts, Trump likened recent calls to slow its development, on the grounds that its rapid development poses an existential threat to humankind, as a “globalist scheme” hatched by the same forces he blamed for warnings of climate change, a premise he has long erroneously labelled a “hoax”.
Part of the answer, he said, was to change its name. Henceforth it would cease to be called “artificial” (“it makes it sound fake – and it’s not fake”) and would be called “super intelligence” in all US government documents.
“Welcome to the new world of super intelligence,” he said. “Let’s see if that goes. It’s much more accurate. Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, maybe I don’t.”

articles.title_orig: Judge temporarily overturns Trump's White House media ban
articles.title_zh: Judge temporarily overturns Trump's White House media ban
articles.content_orig:
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to immediately reinstate access to the White House for three news organisations barred from the building last week by the president.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their access restored for 14 days, the judge ruled, saying the ban "likely violated their constitutional due process rights". Some reporters from the outlets said they had been turned away on Thursday morning.
The three outlets launched a legal challenge after their reporters were denied access last weekend.
The administration had defended the move in court, accusing the outlets of publishing false information and threatening national security.
It was unclear whether all reporters from the outlets would be readmitted to the White House early on Thursday morning. CNN said some of their reporters had been denied, and others allowed in. MS Now said a reporter was also stopped from entering and a Politico reporter said they had been turned away.
The White House is yet to comment on the ruling, and lawyers acting for the president may take further legal action.
Judge Timothy Kelly ruled , external CNN, Politico and MS NOW were "likely to succeed" in showing the White House had not exercised "adequate due process" in implementing the ban.
He also cast doubt on the Trump administration's arguments that the bans were motivated by national security concerns, pointing out the president made no mention of that in his initial announcement.
When President Donald Trump announced the ban on Friday, he accused the three news outlets of writing "fake news" and "fictions and lies" in their coverage of him and his team.
The ruling continued: "The record lacks factual support for Defendants' contention that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the Court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds."
In its defence of the ban in a court filing on Tuesday, the Trump administration cited a number of articles published by the outlets, including some about construction at the White House, including work on a new ballroom.
The judge said that "in most cases" the stories the White House took issue with were written by journalists who "did not even hold card passes" - and in the remaining cases, the Trump administration did not demonstrate "reason to believe that the reporter's possession of the hard pass was integral to the stories identified".
In its original filing, the Trump administration cited declarations from defence department officials supporting the ban - but the judge said they had "no direct knowledge of how reporters operate in the White House, or about any of the facts at issue here".
Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, told CNN , external : "This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law."
On Monday, major US TV networks pulled out of White House pool duties in protest at the ban. The arrangement sees media organisations share material with each other to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.
Forty-nine media organisations - including CBS News, The New York Times and Fox News - also filed a legal brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico's lawsuit.
Trump frequently criticises news organisations, and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the BBC.
Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multi-million-dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

articles.title_zh: Melania Trump’s home-country leader rips UN ‘double standards’ as Trump promise is revealed
articles.content_orig:
PM Janez Janša says the UN's focus on Gaza has overshadowed other global crises, criticizes Europe's approach to Iran and discusses Slovenia's special relationship with the US through First Lady Melania Trump.
UNITED NATIONS - Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša accused the United Nations of applying double standards to global conflicts, arguing that the international community's focus on Gaza has overshadowed Russia's war in Ukraine and other humanitarian crises, while revealing that President Donald Trump has promised to visit Slovenia, the homeland of first lady Melania Trump .
Speaking exclusively to Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Janša said the international body must give greater attention to conflicts beyond the Middle East rather than concentrating its diplomatic efforts on a single crisis.
"We have to get rid of double standards," Janša said, calling for the U.N. to apply its available diplomatic and security tools equally instead of putting its attention, money and energy into one conflict while neglecting others.
MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT
Right-wing Slovenian Democratic Party (SDS) leader Janez Janša addresses the media after his investiture vote as Slovenia's Prime Minister at the National Assembly in Ljubljana on May 22, 2026. (Jure Makovec / AFP via Getty Images)
The Slovenian leader said he was struck by how extensively Gaza dominated speeches during the opening of the General Assembly , while Ukraine, a war much closer to his country's borders, received comparatively less attention.
For Slovenia and other European countries, he said, Russia's invasion represents an immediate security threat, with no clear indication that Moscow is prepared to negotiate an end to the fighting.
Janša argued that the U.N. was established to prevent such conflicts and should not allow its attention to be consumed by one region.
He also pointed to the persecution of Christians in Nigeria and other humanitarian crises, arguing that the international body must recognize that different countries face different security and humanitarian challenges.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
An office building burns following a Russian drone attack in central Odesa, Ukraine, on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Michael Shtekel/AP)
Janša said he intends to raise the issue during his own address to the General Assembly, scheduled for Thursday.
His criticism comes as Slovenia undergoes a significant shift in its foreign policy, particularly toward Israel.
Under the previous government of Prime Minister Robert Golob, Slovenia recognized Palestinian statehood in June 2024 and imposed an arms embargo on Israel in July 2025. The government defended those measures as necessary to protect Palestinian civilians and uphold international law.
Since returning to power, Janša has sought to strengthen Slovenia's relationship with Israel, marking a shift from the previous government's more critical approach toward the Jewish state.
Earlier this month, Israel opened its first resident embassy in Slovenia, while Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar visited the country for talks aimed at expanding political and economic cooperation. The two governments also signed a cooperation program covering education, science, culture, youth and sports through 2030.
Janša described his government's approach as a return to the traditionally good relations between the two countries rather than a dramatic diplomatic realignment.
US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS
President Donald Trump and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shake hands as they meet on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City in this handout released September 22, 2026. (Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout via Reuters)
He also criticized European governments that, in his view, have failed to recognize the broader strategic connections between Iran , Russia and the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Janša said he has supported the Iranian opposition for decades and argued that lasting peace in the Middle East would remain elusive without political change in Tehran.
He accused some European governments of applying inconsistent standards by supporting Ukraine while taking positions toward Iran that he believes fail to account for Tehran’s relationship with Moscow, citing Ireland and Spain as well as Slovenia under the previous government before this year’s change in leadership.
Janša also suggested that some European leaders have used the Palestinian issue to divert public attention from domestic economic and political problems, particularly ahead of elections.
The prime minister's visit to New York also provided an opportunity to strengthen Slovenia's relationship with Washington, a relationship that carries a personal dimension because of the country's most prominent American connection: First Lady Melania Trump.
Born in Slovenia in 1970, Melania Trump grew up in the town of Sevnica before moving to the United States and becoming the nation's second foreign-born first lady.
The prime minister praised Melania Trump’s work on initiatives for children, describing her role in the White House as a source of pride for many Slovenians. He said his wife met the first lady for the first time on Tuesday and that he also spoke briefly with President Trump.

According to Janša, he invited Trump to visit Slovenia and received a positive response. "He promised he'll come," Janša told Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict.
Getachew Reda, a cabinet minister and adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched offensives in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.
Earlier, the Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced to enter a "defensive war". The statement followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray.
The two-year war in Tigray ended in 2022 - but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating a peace deal.
It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Ethiopian President Taye Astike Selassie said his country had shown "immense restraint" in its actions despite "interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements", without specifying who those elements were.
He added: "Our message to forces of destruction and mayhem is loud and clear. We urge them to respect the sacred right of the people of the Horn of Africa to live in peace and prosperity."
On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray,  announced an alliance with six other armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa.
Getachew said in a statement shared on social media: "It is rather heartbreaking to learn that, despite efforts by many, including the international community, to avoid yet another round of war in Tigray, the TPLF leadership early this morning launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara."
The adviser to Prime Minster Abiy Ahmed previously led Tigray's interim administration, but he fell out with the TPLF in 2025 and joined the federal government.
Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.
Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.
This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.
A resident of Mekelle told the BBC's Newsday programme there had been no clashes in the city, unlike in the previous war, with most fighting happening elsewhere.
"Mekelle is calm, except the stress from the people," said the resident, only identified as Fitsum for his safety. He added that the biggest problem was economic, with people not having enough cash.
"People are in a mood where they are distressed because it's been so difficult, so tough. The last seven or eight months the government has been denying budgets to the civil servants and all the banks were running out of cash."
Fitsum said people had been relying on mobile banking but with the risk of communications being cut off, "people are going to be in grave danger because there is almost no cash".
With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he told the BBC.
The chairperson of the Africa Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, has called for an "immediate de-escalation" and for both sides to resume talks.
The US ambassador to Ethiopia condemned the TPLF for making "the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive", describing it as an "unwinnable fight".
On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities.
The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes starting at around 03:30.
"This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said.
Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools.
He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces.
But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun.
The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not commented on the alleged strikes.
On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an "open invasion" of the region, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity.
It further accused the government of violating international humanitarian and human rights laws, saying public services and critical infrastructure had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid.
It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, the AU-brokered deal that formally ended the conflict in November 2022.
In July, Prime Minister Abiy accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament.
Just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy.
There have also been reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s FDA pick to face scrutiny over abortion pill access at confirmation hearing
articles.title_zh: Trump’s FDA pick to face scrutiny over abortion pill access at confirmation hearing
articles.content_orig:
Dr. Heidi Overton, a fierce opponent of abortion rights, is set to appear before senators Thursday for her confirmation hearing to lead the Food and Drug Administration.
The hearing before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee comes as the FDA faces pressure from Republicans, including the committee’s chair, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., to tighten access to the abortion pill mifepristone.
Cassidy, who is a key vote in Overton’s confirmation, has been pushing the administration to reverse a Biden-era rule that allows mifepristone to be prescribed via telemedicine and sent through the mail.
In a committee report published last month , Cassidy accused the makers of mifepristone of failing to meet their legal responsibilities to ensure compliance with FDA safety regulations, particularly when the pills are sold online through third-party providers. At a hearing in January , Cassidy called on Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the previous FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary, to complete a safety review that they both promised during their confirmation hearings. In June, the FDA said it launched a new safety study on mifepristone.
Art Caplan, the head of the medical ethics division at NYU Grossman School of Medicine in New York City, said Overton’s views on abortion appear to align with Cassidy’s.
Overton, a preventive medicine physician, currently serves as a domestic policy official in the White House. Prior to that, she worked as chief policy officer at the conservative think tank America First Policy Institute, where she praised the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade and called for strict restrictions on medication abortion, claiming that it is “ dangerous to women .” (Studies have shown that the drug , even when taken at home, is safe and effective.)
If confirmed, Overton would take over an agency that has been without a permanent commissioner since Makary resigned in May, in part over the administration’s decision to authorize several fruit-flavored vapes for adults.
As commissioner, Overton would serve as a key ally to Kennedy, whose department oversees the FDA. Overton is a proponent of Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement. She also appeared alongside President Donald Trump in August when he announced an executive order aimed at reducing the number of vaccines routinely recommended for children. Trump nominated her to lead the agency days later.
Senators are likely to grill her about her own views on vaccines, according to Dorit Reiss, a professor of law and vaccine policy expert at the University of California Law San Francisco.
On CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday, Cassidy — who has also aggressively questioned and pressed several Trump administration nominees on vaccines — said Overton must acknowledge that Trump’s claim that the measles vaccine is lethal is “absurd” when she appears before his committee. Trump made the comment during the August signing of his vaccine executive order.
“I think she made it clear she’s a supporter of Kennedy’s vaccine agenda, at least,” Reiss said. “Dr. Overton seems like another example of an appointee who is, primarily, appointed for political opinions, without an emphasis on qualifications.”
Overton, Reiss said, doesn’t appear to have expertise in clinical trials, managing an agency or any of the products the FDA regulates.
“It’s reasonable for an administration to want someone sympathetic to their views,” Reiss said, “but FDA commissioner is a hard job that requires the ability to manage a large and complex agency that does important work.”
“As an MD/PhD who helped President Trump deliver on Operation Warp Speed during his first term, Dr. Heidi Overton will ensure that policymaking is guided solely by Gold Standard Science at the FDA,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement.
Dr. Stephen Ostroff, a former acting FDA commissioner, said food safety will be another major issue waiting for her at the FDA.
The agency has spent much of the summer responding to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks and recalls, including a massive cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce that sickened more than 12,000 people across multiple states.
The outbreak has also raised questions about how quickly the FDA can trace contaminated food back to its source and whether the agency has enough staff to respond to outbreaks after thousands of employees left or were laid off over the past year.
“After the experience of the past 18 months, it’s very important to restore public and industry confidence that decisions being made by FDA, including those by leadership, are science-based, transparent and consistent,” Ostroff said.

On Monday, we reported on an issue where iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max users were seeing their phone freeze and reboot following a failed Face ID attempt. To us, it appeared to be a software glitch rather than an inherent hardware fault.
Apple has now confirmed to 9to5Mac that a software update to address this problem is in the works, and should be available early next week.
Although the bug did not seemingly affect all users, it was reasonably widespread based on social media and 9to5Mac reader reports.
At the time, we reproduced the problem on an iPhone 18 Pro device by obscuring our face with our hand as we attempted a Face ID authentication to access the Passwords app. The phone simply stops responding to touch input, and hard reboots after a few seconds. You could then find a panic log in the iPhone Analytics section of the Settings app.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max feature a redesigned Face ID sensor system, where the Infrared camera has moved behind the under the screen near where the clock is rendered in the status bar, resulting in a 25% smaller visible Dynamic Island.
As we reported earlier in the week, some customers had already attempted to resolve the rebooting problem by swapping their phone with a new device at Apple, thinking it was a hardware fault. To reiterate, this is not necessary with a software fix now confirmed to be on the way.
On a somewhat related note, Apple also just released watchOS 27.0.1 to fix a random restart issue with Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi summit: Here’s what’s on the agenda, and why it matters
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi summit: Here’s what’s on the agenda, and why it matters
articles.content_orig:
China’s leader Xi Jinping is expected to hold highly anticipated talks with United States President Donald Trump in Washington on Thursday, as both sides seek to ease trade tensions and discuss increasingly capable artificial intelligence (AI) systems.
On Wednesday evening, Trump and US First Lady Melania Trump greeted Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, with a rare red carpet welcome. No US president had previously welcomed a visiting guest personally at the base in six decades.
Earlier in the day, China’s state broadcaster CCTV reported that Xi and Peng were being accompanied by the president’s closest aide and adviser, Cai Qi, and Foreign Minister Wang Yi.
The White House said the talks scheduled for Thursday would mark “a significant milestone in the relationship between the two countries”.
But the state visit – Xi’s first to the US in more than a decade – is likely to touch on multiple points of tension, including the US-Israel war on Iran, the fallout from Trump’s tariffs and the threat of war over the island of Taiwan, which China claims as its territory.
Trump met Xi on his arrival at Joint Base Andrews. But the main event is on Thursday morning, when Xi will receive a ceremonial welcome at the White House, accompanied by a military flyover and nearly 500 military personnel.
After the two leaders hold talks during the day, Trump will host a state dinner for Xi at the White House. This event is expected to include chiefs of companies important in both markets, such as Apple’s Tim Cook, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and OpenAI’s Sam Altman.
The visit will wrap up on Friday morning when the two presidential couples will have tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives to round off the trip.
Instead ⁠of a joint news conference or statement at the end, the countries are expected to issue separate announcements highlighting what each side hopes to convey to its own domestic audience.
Before the main meeting on Thursday, the two sides have already walked away from an imminent cliff: their current 11-month trade truce was set to expire in November, but has now been extended until January 10, giving their negotiating teams more time to hammer out a broader deal.
The US-Israel war on Iran is also likely to ⁠feature prominently in the discussions. Beijing has maintained close ties with Tehran, but it is unclear whether a meeting with Xi will do anything to help Trump break the ongoing deadlock in the conflict. Washington may hope that Beijing could use its influence over Tehran, observers say, but Trump has so far maintained he sees no need to seek China’s help.
The two countries are also likely to talk more about the race to develop AI, as they are in fierce competition but mindful of growing dangers. The US has proposed a new “notification mechanism” with China to alert each other of any AI incident serious enough to threaten national security.
China is also expected to raise the issue of Taiwan. In December, the Trump administration approved an $11bn arms sale to Taiwan, the largest ever, but a second package, worth some $14bn, has been on hold for months. Trump has described the arms sales as a “very good negotiating chip”.
Trump is also expected to seek the release of some Americans and others imprisoned in China, after securing the July release of Pastor Ezra Jin , a Chinese national jailed as part of the 2025 crackdown on underground churches in China. Trump had raised the pastor’s case with Xi in May.
Trump’s decision to greet Xi personally upon arrival shows how far the US president is going to honour China’s leader, observers say. During a TV interview, Melania Trump said her husband had decided to greet Xi because they “have a great relationship”.
“He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect,” she said of Xi and his wife during the interview with Fox News.
Despite the conciliatory tones, however, the two leaders’ ties have been strained by a trade war that began shortly after Trump returned to office for a second presidential term in January 2025.
The US president imposed a 10 percent duty on Chinese goods over fentanyl and immigration concerns, while China responded with levies on US coal, liquefied natural gas (LNG), crude oil and autos, and curbs on exports of five rare-earth metals that are essential for the manufacture of defence equipment and clean energy.
Both sides escalated rapidly, with tariffs reaching triple digits and Beijing also warning its citizens against US travel. China also threatened to impose curbs on the export of seven more rare-earth metals late last year.
That was put on hold when Trump and Xi struck a trade truce following talks in South Korea in October 2025. When the US president travelled to China in May this year, they announced plans to create a Board of Trade and Investment, ⁠while Xi agreed to purchases of Boeing jets and US farm products.
But Trump has since imposed new 12.5 percent tariffs on goods from 60 trading partners, including China, over allegations that those countries failed to curb imports made ⁠by forced labour.
Thursday’s meeting at the White House marks the two leaders’ third in-person meeting in a little less than a year amid what has been described as a reprieve in hostilities.
Both sides continue to test one another while avoiding an escalation. During Trump’s state visit, the two sides agreed to “a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability”, a diplomatic framework often referred to as “constructive strategic stability”.
The meeting will prove a further test of whether such a posture can hold in light of each side’s competing interests.
This balancing act could yield deals to reduce tariffs in specific sectors, cooperate on drug trafficking, and expand military-to-military dialogue.
It could also set the course for steady, long-term development of bilateral relations and confirm cooperation as the mainstay.

articles.title_orig: College football picks ATS Week 4: Texas-Tennessee, Ole Miss-Florida and more - The Athletic
articles.title_zh: College football picks ATS Week 4: Texas-Tennessee, Ole Miss-Florida and more - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Heading into Week 4, college football's top tier is starting to settle into place. Expected contenders like Texas A&M and Oklahoma are on the way out, while Ole Miss and USC can prove themselves with big wins this upcoming Saturday.
At the top of the weekend is a heavyweight battle in the Group of Six between two teams that nearly pulled major upsets against Big Ten foes. The winner takes control of the non-power race. There are plenty of other prove-it games between postseason hopefuls, especially as the SEC tries to work itself out.
Here are six games in Week 4 with major College Football Playoff and conference championship implications.
Both Western Michigan and Boise State have played electric nonconference slates to this point, and each nearly pulled an upset over a major-ranked Big Ten foe (and WMU did win). And now, the driver's seat of the Group of Six CFP race is on the line in Kalamazoo.
The Broncos of Kalamazoo have emerged as the class of the MAC in recent years after a wave of investment under coach Lance Taylor. The program was able to keep a decent amount of the roster together despite poachers. The Idaho-based Broncos laid the model for many such programs with their retention of Ashton Jeanty. Plenty of other players on the roster are back and ready.
Boise State is a seven-point favorite heading into the matchup, but that just sets up perfectly for Western Michigan to spoil the party. The loser of this game is all but eliminated from playoff contention.
Big Ten championship implications are on the line in Los Angeles as USC tries to break through against the Ducks. A few bad performances for Oregon are forgivable, but this is the moment when the program has to quickly elevate to a national caliber. A second loss would be devastating with a road trip to No. 1 Ohio State left on the schedule.
USC experienced a reset under Lincoln Riley, and now prepares to take the first steps back towards contention. The Trojans cruised to 4-0 for the second straight season, but failed to break through last year. With three top-13 opponents ahead, USC also has to deliver.
Ole Miss elevated itself firmly into the playoff race with a win over LSU, but the Rebels don't get long to enjoy it before traveling to face Florida in The Swamp. The Gators are fresh off a big win over Auburn and enter the rankings for the first time since losing to South Florida last season.
SEC schedules set up brutally for nearly every program, and this opportunity is especially big for the Gators. Florida faces all of No. 1 Texas, No. 2 Georgia and No. 4 Ole Miss this season. To make the postseason, they'll have to beat at least one, and this is the only home game among them.
Behind Ohio State and Indiana, the race for the top of the Big Ten is wide open. Oregon and USC have both been inconsistent, and battle on Saturday. That leaves an opening for either the 2023 national champion Wolverines or an outsider like Iowa.
For Iowa, the time is crucial. The Hawkeyes are surging behind star running back Kamari Moulton and wide receiver transfer Tony Diaz. There's optimism that this could be one of the best Iowa teams in years. They can elevate themselves in the Big House.
This could be a serious loser-goes-home game. The Tigers and Aggies are both coming off difficult losses: the Tigers to Ole Miss, and Texas A&M at home against Kentucky. Both offenses are facing major questions after disappointing performances.
LSU's defense is probably the best unit in the game, especially going against a Texas A&M offense still lacking identity. The loser of this game will likely pick up a second SEC loss, essentially eliminating them from SEC championship consideration. Both also still have games remaining against No. 1 Texas and No. 8 Alabama.
Is Texas real? The Longhorns looked inconsistent during a lackluster win over UTSA, with the offense mustering only 4.8 yards per play. Tennessee hasn't yet played a quality opponent, but the Volunteers are positioned well to take advantage of yet another slow start for Texas.
Tennessee is 3-0 and is averaging just shy of 300 yards rushing per game. An upset victory would help set the tone for another playoff-caliber season.

Dreams do come true. That’s certainly the case for Nene Royal, the precocious talent who was tonight crowned winner of America’s Got Talent .
The 16-year-old Thai singer and guitarist has electrified audiences — and AGT ‘s judges — throughout this 21st season.
When it mattered most, the teen sensation captured the heart of the nation. She won America’s vote and captured the title, announced during the two-hour results show which aired Wednesday night (Sept. 23) on NBC .
As the champion, Royal earns more than bragging rights. She scores the $1 million grand prize and a headlining spot in a live show in Las Vegas.
See latest videos, charts and news
Special guests and performers during the live results show included Josh Groban, Lele Pons, REI AMI, Steve Aoki, and Linkin Park who, following America’s Vote, collaborated with Royal for a performance of “The Emptiness Machine.”
Hailing from Phuket, Thailand, Royal picked up the guitar at age seven and has always dreamed of being a “superstar on tour,” she explained during the auditions phase of AGT . She delivered the goods in a massive way, by belting-out a reinterpreted cover of The Cranberries mid-‘90s protest anthem “Zombie.”
With her spot in the quarterfinals, Royal proved she was no one-hit wonder. Her cover of Soundgarden’s “Black Hole Sun” was such a blast, it earned Mel B’s Golden Buzzer. With that, the youngster advanced to the finals.
For her performance in the season 21 finale, Nene reimagined the White Stripes’ classic 2000s number “Seven Nation Army,” grinding Jack White’s iconic riff into a heavy weapon and introducing a fresh guitar solo. The youngster wore a traditional dress, emblazoned with the words “Nene Thailand.”
“Well, I’m glad I pressed my Golden Buzzer,” Mel B remarked after the amps were turned off. “Because not only do you have such mysterious, mystical stage presence, you’re from the best place in the world, Phuket, Thailand…and what you’re bringing to this competition is so unique and you’re only 16 years old. If you don’t win this, I am going to sell Howie’s new house.”
Sofía Vergara said she was confident that the “world is going crazy because there is nothing like you right now, you are unique.”
Howie Mandel spoke last. Nene, he enthused, is “the biggest, most talented, most viral talent to be on that stage…you should win. Give her the million, America.”
The veteran actor spoke truth. It was a winning performance. For the record, magician Geno Ploeger came in second, and magician group Hundred Fingers completed the podium in third place.

articles.title_orig: Packers Wire staff predictions: Week 3 vs. Falcons
articles.title_zh: Packers Wire staff predictions: Week 3 vs. Falcons
articles.content_orig:
The Green Bay Packers will attempt to win a second consecutive game and get to 2-1 to start 2026 while also extending the team's record home opener win streak to 14 games when the Atlanta Falcons come to Lambeau Field for "Thursday Night Football" in Week 3. Matt LaFleur's team has looked shaky through two weeks, but a chance to come home and play a struggling Falcons team could be just what the doctor ordered.
Here’s how the staff at Packers Wire believes the Week 3 showdown with the Falcons will go down:
On a scale of 1-10, my confidence level in a Packers victory is not high, maybe a 5 or 6. If the Falcons had any kind of pulse, this would feel like a true toss up game given the state of the offensive line, and how so much of what has ailed the Packers is centered on the offensive line's play through two weeks. That said, if there's a more troubled offensive team entering Week 3, it's the Falcons, who are returning their quarterback but still have massive problems. Overall, the Packers defense has been a real strength, so even if Green Bay's offense struggles to sustain drives once again, I think a takeaway or two will probably swing the game in the right direction. Winning ugly might just be the way forward until the rebuilt offensive line settles in. Defense. Special teams. Don't mess it up on offense. That should be the plan for Thursday night.
Green Bay’s offense has looked rough through the first two weeks, and it’s unclear when/if it will get better. Losing Jayden Reed for an unspecified amount of time and Zach Bako-Bewele for the season won’t help. The Packers’ offensive grade from Pro Football Focus is 55.8, tied for last with the Falcons. I’m not expecting a high-scoring affair Thursday night. Michael Penix Jr. is set to make his season debut for the Falcons and could show signs of rust. Atlanta can try feeding Bijan Robinson, but Green Bay’s run defense is eighth in rushing yards allowed per game. The Falcons' defense is first in rushing yards allowed per game, but the Packers haven’t been able to run the ball much anyway. Green Bay has the better quarterback, but the pass-blocking hasn’t given Jordan Love enough time to operate the offense efficiently—he currently has the lowest completion percentage (52.1%) in the league among quarterbacks with at least 30 pass attempts. Atlanta’s pass rush has already generated 48 pressures, but I still like the Packers in their home opener.
The home opener should provide a friendlier environment for Green Bay’s offense to hopefully find some kind of rhythm, but missing Zach Bako-Bewele and Aaron Banks will not help the already worrisome O-line, and the Falcons have been generating pressure at a high rate, even if it has been more of the slow burn variety. Even on a short week and without two starting O-linemen and Jayden Reed, I’m backing them to put up more points this time around, as well as Jonathan Gannon continuing to tweak his defense to hold Michael Penix and the Atlanta offense in check. The Packers need a ‘get right’ game, and Thursday night presents a big opportunity.
The Packers offense needs to get rolling and it starts by getting Tucker Kraft more involved. Atlanta’s defense just gave up two touchdowns to Darren Waller and in week one they gave up a touchdown to Pat Freiermuth. I fully expect the pride of Timber Lake to have a monster game in primetime to remind everyone just how special he is. On the flip side Green Bay’s defense, along with their special teams play is the reason they won last week. They could turn in their best performance of the young season in front of the Lambeau Field crowd. Give me the Packers by double digits.

articles.title_orig: Dolly Parton's Estate Secures Restraining Order Against Nephew Over 'Demands for Payment'
articles.title_zh: Dolly Parton's Estate Secures Restraining Order Against Nephew Over 'Demands for Payment'
articles.content_orig:
A day after Dolly Parton ’s trust accused her nephew of interfering with its business relationships through “threats, intimidation and coercion,” a Tennessee judge granted the estate a temporary restraining order against him, citing a series of emails and other communications that allegedly paired “threats with demands for payment.”
In an order issued Wednesday and obtained by Rolling Stone , Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles of Nashville Chancery Court directed Parton’s nephew, Bryan Seaver, to stay at least 1,000 feet from estate employees and business partners, remain off private property owned by the estate, and refrain from disruptive or harassing conduct.
Attempts to reach Seaver for comment were not immediately successful Wednesday. He is the relative who announced Parton’s death in a prerecorded video posted to her Instagram account that drew millions of reactions. According to court filings, Seaver previously worked for private military contractors and later provided security for Parton and her properties through his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, which is also subject to the temporary restraining order.
The judge’s order issued Wednesday cites several written communications filed as exhibits with the estate’s complaint on Tuesday. In multiple messages excerpted in the ruling, Seaver allegedly threatened Danny Nozell, the sole manager of She’s Alive LLC, the company that Parton designated to control her professional property and business interests after her death.
“I’m going to destroy the entire brand if you don’t get these [Dollywood business partners] out of our bit,” Seaver allegedly wrote in one text on Aug. 19, about a week before Parton’s death at age 80 .
“I just sold 29 million dollars worth of ammo to Haiti. I’m not exactly a media person, Danny. I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary,” Seaver purportedly wrote in another text after Parton died.
“Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do,” reads another message attributed to Seaver and cited in the ruling. “All I have is animosity and memory. But I’m going to spend the next times I have on earth ratfucking anyone that has ever betrayed my family.”
Judge Myles wrote that the statements were significant “not merely because of their language in isolation, but also because they were made in conjunction with statements threatening specific individuals and business interests associated with Ms. Parton’s professional property and estate.”
The judge also said Seaver had “expressly connected threatened interference with Ms. Parton’s commercial interests to a demand for payment.” The ruling cited another alleged message from Seaver: “I’m going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or fucking pay me.”
Myles set a follow-up court hearing for Oct. 7. At this preliminary stage, however, she wrote that the messages appeared to demonstrate a “repeated course of conduct” in which Seaver identified specific people or interests and allegedly “coupled those threats with demands for payment or other action” while invoking “his claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate.”
Seaver was removed from his security role connected to Parton’s business on Sept. 15, according to a letter from lawyers representing She’s Alive that was filed in the business-interference case. The letter, obtained by Rolling Stone , said the termination did not affect Seaver’s separate interest as a beneficiary of the trust. If Seaver chooses to fight the restraining order, he must file a response by Oct. 2, Myles said. The Oct. 7 hearing will address any further relief sought by the estate.
In a statement to TMZ on Tuesday, Seaver defended his text messages and said they were taken out of context. “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments,” he said. “However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.”
